settings.question: What's the difference between an ST trailer tire and an LT light-truck tire?
settings.answer: ST stands for Special Trailer — these tires are engineered specifically for being towed (not driven under power). They have stiffer sidewalls to handle sway, higher load ratings for their size, and a tread compound optimized for towing-temperature heat. LT tires (Light Truck) are designed for vehicles that drive under power and have to handle steering, braking, and acceleration. Don't substitute one for the other: an LT tire on a trailer wears unevenly and an ST tire on a truck will overheat at highway speed.

settings.question: What size trailer tires do I need?
settings.answer: The size is printed on the sidewall of your existing tire — it'll start with ST followed by numbers like ST205/75R15 or ST235/80R16. The most common Calgary trailer sizes we stock or can source same-day: ST205/75R15 (small utility, boat trailers), ST225/75R15 (mid utility, common landscaping trailers), ST235/80R16 (heavy utility, larger boat trailers), and ST235/85R16 (most RV and fifth-wheel trailers). Bring your trailer or send a photo of the sidewall and we'll match it.

settings.question: Should I get radial, bias-ply, or all-steel radial trailer tires?
settings.answer: For 95% of Calgary trailer owners — radial is the right answer. Standard ST radials run cooler, last about 40% longer than bias-ply, and ride smoother. Step up to all-steel radial (Load Range G or H, 14–16 ply) if you tow heavy: fifth-wheels, gooseneck trailers, fully-loaded utility trailers, or anything over 7,000 lbs GVWR. Bias-ply is legacy construction — only consider it for very light trailers (boat trailers under 2,000 lbs) where the cheaper price wins.

settings.question: How long do trailer tires last in Calgary?
settings.answer: Trailer tires age out before they wear out. Even unused, the rubber degrades from UV, ozone, and freeze-thaw cycles — Calgary winters and dry summers are particularly hard on parked trailers. Expect 3–5 years of service life regardless of mileage. If your trailer sits all winter and you only tow May through October, you'll get 4–6 seasons. Check the DOT date code on the sidewall (4 digits = week + year) — anything 5+ years old should be inspected; 7+ years should be replaced regardless of tread depth.

settings.question: Can I get trailer tire and wheel assemblies (mounted, balanced, ready-to-bolt-on)?
settings.answer: Yes. We stock complete trailer tire+wheel assemblies in the most common sizes — ST205/75R15 and ST225/75R15 on 5-bolt steel wheels, ST235/80R16 and ST235/85R16 on 6-bolt heavier-duty wheels. Pre-mounted assemblies save you the install fee and get you back on the road faster — popular with boat owners ahead of long-weekend trips and contractors who can't afford trailer downtime.

settings.question: How fast can I tow on trailer tires?
settings.answer: Standard ST tires are speed-rated to 65 mph (105 km/h). Premium all-steel radials are rated up to 75 mph (120 km/h) or higher — check the speed-rating letter on the sidewall (L = 75 mph, M = 81 mph). On Alberta highways like the QE2 to Edmonton or Trans-Canada into BC, staying at posted limits is usually fine for premium tires, but if you tow heavy or fast routinely, factor speed rating into your tire choice. Underrated tires at highway speed are the #1 cause of trailer-tire blowouts.

settings.heading: What makes a trailer tire different
settings.intro:
A trailer tire isn't just a passenger tire on a smaller wheel. It's a fundamentally different product — built for being towed, not driven. Trailer (ST) tires have stiffer sidewalls, higher load ratings for their size, and a rubber compound formulated for towing heat. Mixing them up with light-truck (LT) or passenger (P-metric) tires is one of the most common mistakes we see in the shop — and it shortens tire life dramatically.

Here's what sets an ST trailer tire apart:
settings.outro: Wrong sizing, wrong load range, or aged-out tires are the three failure modes that put trailers on the shoulder of Highway 2 every summer. Match the tire to the trailer and the load, replace before the rubber cracks, and you'll never sit on the side of the road waiting for a flatbed.

settings.text: Polyester body plies + 2 steel belts under the tread. The right pick for 95% of Calgary trailer owners — utility, boat, small landscaping. Quiet, smooth, ~40% longer life than bias-ply on paved roads.

settings.lead: All-Steel ST Radial (Load Range G or H, 14–16 ply)
settings.text: Steel body plies AND steel belts. Runs 20–30°F cooler at highway speed than bias-ply, carries heavier loads without sidewall flex. The right pick for RVs, fifth-wheels, gooseneck trailers, dump trailers, and anything over 7,000 lbs GVWR.

Legacy construction — cord plies criss-cross diagonally. Cheaper than radial, but runs hotter, wears faster, and rides rougher. Only consider for very light, occasional-use trailers (small boat trailers under 2,000 lbs) where the price difference actually matters.

Some heavy-duty trailers spec LT tires instead of ST — typically commercial trailers with dual-axle dual-wheel setups. We can source LT (BFGoodrich, Michelin, Toyo) when the trailer manufacturer specifies it. Don't substitute on your own.
